title: Cryogenic Multiplexing Control Chip for Superconducting Quantum Processor
authors: Rutian Huang, Xiao Geng, Xinyu Wu, Genting Dai, Liangliang Yang, Jianshe Liu, Wei Chen
abstract: This paper proposes a scheme and design of cryogenic multiplexing control chip (MCC) which enables one microwave cable to control many superconducting qubits. Designed based on adjustable inductor, MCC is a non-reciprocal device which generates microwave signals between 4 and 8 GHz and constructs XY control circuit to operate qubits. The effects of filters, isolators, power splitters, qubits and load impedance on MCC are analyzed in the frequency-domain simulation. And in time-domain simulation, the response time, Gaussian pulses, single-sideband, amplitude and frequency compensation of MCC are examined. The MCC can be integrated with the superconducting qubits on the same package at 20 mK temperature stage, and output specific microwave pulses used to drive the superconducting qubits without crosstalks. The MCC can greatly reduce the number of microwave control lines and is beneficial to the development of large-scale superconducting quantum processor.
summary: This paper proposes and simulates a Cryogenic Multiplexing Control Chip (MCC) to solve the wiring bottleneck in large quantum processors. The MCC uses advanced microwave components like tunable isolators to allow a single cable to control many qubits without crosstalk. This significantly advances the feasibility of building large-scale superconducting quantum computers.
main_problem: The paper addresses the interconnect bottleneck in scaling superconducting quantum processors due to the need for numerous, lossy microwave control lines.
main_result: The proposed Cryogenic Multiplexing Control Chip (MCC) successfully enables one microwave cable to control multiple superconducting qubits while mitigating crosstalks.
method: The authors used both frequency-domain (S-parameter analysis) and time-domain simulations to model the MCC's signal processing capabilities.
model_or_system: The system is a Cryogenic Multiplexing Control Chip (MCC) designed to operate at 20 mK, utilizing adjustable inductors, power splitters, and non-reciprocal isolators to multiplex and demultiplex microwave control signals (4-8 GHz).
key_observables: S-parameters ($S_{ij}$), signal waveforms (Gaussian pulses, CW), crosstalk levels, and frequency shifts.
important_parameters: Operating temperature (20 mK), frequency range (4-8 GHz), and the required isolation degree ($I_{iso}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the MCC can be integrated on the same package as the qubits, and that specific BPF types (Chebyshev) provide optimal filtering.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the MCC circuit diagram, time-domain signal generation (USB/LSB), and frequency-domain comparisons showing the effectiveness of different filters and isolators in minimizing crosstalk.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the interconnect bottleneck, then detailing the MCC design, followed by rigorous frequency-domain modeling using S-parameters, and concluding with time-domain simulations demonstrating pulse generation and signal integrity.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles a critical engineering challenge—scalability—for superconducting quantum processors, which is a major focus area in quantum information science.

Fig. 4 shows the system-level circuit diagram of MCC in the time-domain simulation, where SSB microwave sig- nals are employed. In the left red box, a microwave source of single-tone is send to the local oscillator (LO) signal ports of four IQ Mixers via power splitters. By adjust- ing the Ii(t) and Qi(t) (i=1-4) input signals of IQ mixers, four SSB microwave signals are produced. The synthesiz- ing signals are combined into one microwave line through power splitters, thus completing the multiplexing (MUX) process. In the right box is the MCC device, which de- multiplexes (DEMUX) four signal-tones into four chan- nels for independent control of four qubits.
